Tomato___Early_blight.description: A common fungal disease of tomato and potato. It starts on the older, lower leaves and moves up the plant. Badly infected leaves turn brown and fall off.
Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms: Small dark spots on lower leaves that grow into round brown spots with target-like rings. The area around each spot often turns yellow.
guidance: Remove leaves with spots and bury or burn them. Do not compost them.
Water at the base of the plant and use mulch so soil does not splash onto the leaves.
Stake the plants and leave space between them so the leaves dry faster.
Do not plant tomatoes or peppers in the same spot for two years.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: A fast-spreading disease of tomato and potato that is worst in cool, wet weather. It can destroy plants within days once it takes hold.
Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms: Irregular, water-soaked patches that turn light brown, often starting on the upper leaves. In humid weather, white fuzzy growth can appear under the leaves.
guidance: Remove and destroy infected plants and fruit straight away to slow the spread.
Avoid wetting the leaves when watering, and water early in the day.
Choose resistant varieties when planting again.
Ask a local agriculture officer before using any fungicide, as treatment works best before infection.

Tomato___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this leaf.
guidance: Keep checking the older, lower leaves, where many diseases start.
Water at the base of the plant and keep the leaves dry.
Leave space between plants so air can flow.
Remove weeds and fallen plant debris around the plants.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease of tomato and pepper that spreads quickly in warm, humid weather. It is hard to control once it is established, so prevention is important.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small yellow-green spots with a water-soaked edge. The spots join together, turn brown and dry, and can leave holes and torn leaf edges.
guidance: Start with healthy, inspected seedlings.
Do not handle or work with plants while the leaves are wet.
Remove infected plant debris after the season, and control nearby weeds.
Do not plant tomatoes or peppers in the same spot in the following year.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: A fungal disease that thrives in very humid air, especially in greenhouses and high tunnels. It usually starts on the lower leaves.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale green or yellow spots on the upper side of the leaf, with olive-green, velvety mould on the underside. Badly affected leaves die.
guidance: Improve air flow by spacing plants and opening greenhouse sides or vents.
Remove infected leaves and plants and dispose of them away from the garden.
Clean tools and equipment after working with infected plants.
Choose resistant varieties and clean seed for the next planting.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: A common fungal leaf disease of tomato, favoured by wet weather. It often appears when the first fruits start to form.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Many small, round grey spots with dark edges on the lower leaves. Tiny black dots may be seen inside the spots. Affected leaves turn yellow and die.
guidance: Remove infected leaves during the season, and clear all infected plant parts at the end.
Water at the soil level and keep the leaves dry.
Use mulch to stop soil splashing onto the leaves.
Space plants and remove the lowest leaves once plants are fruiting, to improve air flow.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Damage caused by tiny mites, not by a disease. They feed on the leaves and multiply fast in hot, dry weather.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.symptoms: Fine yellow, white or brown speckles on the leaves, starting low on the plant. Heavy infestations show fine webbing, bronzed leaves and leaf drop.
guidance: Water plants regularly, as dry, stressed plants are more affected.
Spray the plants with water to knock mites off the leaves.
Use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if mites keep spreading.
Ask a local agriculture officer for advice on suitable products.

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: A fungal disease that starts on the older leaves and spreads upward. It spreads fast in warm, wet and windy weather.
Tomato___Target_Spot.symptoms: Small spots with a yellow edge that grow up to about 1 cm and show ring patterns, like a target. Leaves turn yellow, collapse and die.
guidance: Remove some lower branches to improve air flow, and remove infected lower leaves.
Avoid overhead watering.
Keep the area free of weeds.
After harvest, collect and destroy crop remains, and wait three years before planting tomato there again.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: A virus spread by whiteflies. Infected plants cannot be cured, so control focuses on removing infected plants and managing whiteflies.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Young leaves turn yellow between the veins and at the edges, and curl and crumple. Plants become stunted and bushy, and flowers may drop.
guidance: Remove and destroy infected plants to stop the virus spreading.
Check for whiteflies with yellow sticky traps.
Spray neem, pyrethrin or insecticidal soap on the undersides of leaves if whiteflies are many.
Plant resistant varieties and healthy seedlings next time.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A virus that spreads through seed and by handling plants, entering through small wounds. There is no chemical treatment.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Leaves show yellow and green mottled patterns and can be distorted. Plants may be stunted.
guidance: Remove infected plants straight away.
Wash hands and tools after handling plants, and avoid touching plants after using tobacco products.
Use certified disease-free seed.
Grow resistant varieties.

Potato___Early_blight.description: A common fungal disease of potato and tomato. It starts on the older, lower leaves and moves up the plant.
Potato___Early_blight.symptoms: Small dark spots on lower leaves that grow into brown spots with target-like rings, often with yellow tissue around them. Badly infected leaves die.
guidance: Remove leaves with spots and bury or burn them.
Water at the base of the plant and use mulch to stop soil splashing onto leaves.
Space plants well and control weeds so the leaves dry faster.
Do not plant potatoes, tomatoes or peppers in the same spot for two years.

Potato___Late_blight.description: A serious disease of potato and tomato that spreads fast in cool, wet weather. It cannot be cured once symptoms appear, and it can also rot the tubers.
Potato___Late_blight.symptoms: Dark, water-soaked patches on leaves and stems that turn brown. In wet weather, white fuzzy mould can appear under the leaves. Infected tubers get a dry, corky rot.
guidance: Pull out infected plants, seal them in a plastic bag and throw them away. Do not compost them.
Eat tubers from infected plants soon rather than storing them.
At the end of the season, dig up all potatoes, including small pieces left in the soil.
Plant certified seed potatoes, not store-bought ones, and choose resistant varieties.

Potato___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this leaf.
guidance: Check the lower leaves regularly, as early blight starts there.
Water at the base of the plant and keep the leaves dry.
Keep developing tubers covered with soil.
Use certified seed potatoes when planting again.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease of pepper and tomato that spreads in warm, humid weather through rain and overhead watering. It is hard to control once established.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small yellow-green spots with a water-soaked edge. The spots turn brown and dry, leaving holes and a ragged look to the leaves.
guidance: Start with healthy, inspected seedlings.
Avoid overhead watering, and do not handle plants while the leaves are wet.
Remove infected plant debris and control nearby weeds.
Do not plant peppers or tomatoes in the same spot in the following year.

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this leaf.
guidance: Water at the base of the plant and avoid wetting the leaves.
Do not handle plants while the leaves are wet.
Keep the area free of weeds.
Rotate where you plant peppers and tomatoes each year.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: A fungal leaf disease of corn, favoured by warm weather and long periods of high humidity. The fungus survives in corn debris left on the soil.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.symptoms: Small spots with a yellow halo that grow into long, narrow, rectangular grey to brown patches, bounded by the leaf veins.
guidance: Plant resistant hybrids.
Rotate crops instead of planting corn on corn.
Bury or remove corn debris after harvest.
Ask a local agriculture officer before using fungicides.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: A rust disease of corn spread by wind-blown spores. It is favoured by cool, wet weather and heavy dew, and slows down in hot weather.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.symptoms: Small, raised, rust-coloured to dark brown spots (pustules) on both sides of the leaf, which darken as they age.
guidance: Plant resistant corn hybrids, the most effective control.
Check young leaves regularly, as they are the most likely to be infected.
Ask a local agriculture officer about fungicides, which work best when applied early.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: A fungal disease of corn favoured by moderate temperatures and long wet periods. It survives on corn leaf debris.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.symptoms: Long, canoe-shaped grey-green to tan patches, 2.5 to 15 cm long, starting on the lower leaves and moving up the plant.
guidance: Plant resistant hybrids.
Rotate crops and bury or remove corn debris after harvest.
Check lower leaves regularly, especially in wet weather.
Ask a local agriculture officer before using fungicides.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this leaf.
guidance: Plant resistant hybrids where available.
Rotate crops instead of planting corn in the same field every year.
Remove or bury crop debris after harvest.
Check leaves regularly during humid or wet weather.

Apple___Apple_scab.description: A common fungal disease of apple, favoured by cool, wet weather in spring. The fungus survives the winter on fallen infected leaves.
Apple___Apple_scab.symptoms: Small, velvety, olive-green spots, often first on the underside of the leaf, that darken with age. Badly infected leaves twist and drop early.
guidance: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves under the tree at the end of the season.
Prune the tree every year so the leaves dry faster and get more sun.
Plant scab-resistant apple varieties.
Ask a local agriculture officer about fungicide timing in spring.

Apple___Black_rot.description: A fungal disease that affects apple leaves (frogeye leaf spot), fruit and branches. It mostly attacks stressed or weakened trees.
Apple___Black_rot.symptoms: Small round brown spots on the leaves with darker rings, like a frog's eye. Badly infected leaves turn yellow and drop. Fruit can rot black with rings.
guidance: Remove fallen leaves, shrivelled (mummified) fruit and dead branches.
Prune out infected branches between late autumn and early spring.
Keep trees healthy and avoid stress from drought or injury.
Ask a local agriculture officer about fungicides in wet seasons.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: A fungal disease that needs both apple trees and cedar (juniper) trees to complete its life cycle. Spores travel from cedar trees to apple leaves in wet spring weather.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.symptoms: Bright orange to yellow-orange spots on the upper side of the leaves, sometimes with red or yellow edges.
guidance: Remove nearby cedar or juniper trees where possible.
Plant resistant apple varieties.
Prune to open the tree so air and light can move through.
Ask a local agriculture officer about protective fungicides at blossom time.

Apple___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this leaf.
guidance: Prune the tree every year so the leaves dry quickly and get sunlight.
Rake up fallen leaves at the end of the season.
Remove dead branches and shrivelled fruit.
Check young leaves in spring, when many diseases start.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: A fungal disease that grows on the surface of young leaves and shoots. It spreads in warm, dry days with humid nights, and the fungus survives winter on the tree.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White, powdery patches on young leaves, usually on the underside first. Infected leaves curl upward, pucker or look distorted. Fruit can also get white patches near harvest.
guidance: Prune the tree so air and sunlight reach the inner branches.
Avoid too much nitrogen fertiliser, which produces soft new growth the fungus prefers.
Remove suckers and water shoots at the base of the tree.
If the problem returns every year, ask an agriculture officer about sulphur or other approved fungicides.

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: No signs of disease were found on this cherry leaf.
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.symptoms: The leaf is evenly green with no powdery patches, spots or curling.
guidance: Keep pruning for good airflow and sunlight.
Water at the base of the tree, not over the leaves.
Check young leaves regularly, since that is where problems start.

Grape___Black_rot.description: A fungal disease that attacks leaves, shoots and fruit. It spreads in warm, wet weather and survives in shrivelled fruit left on the vine or the ground.
Grape___Black_rot.symptoms: Small, round tan or reddish-brown spots on leaves with a dark border. Tiny black dots form inside the spots. Infected grapes turn brown, then shrivel into hard, black 'mummies'.
guidance: Remove all mummified grapes from the vine and the ground.
Prune and train the vine so leaves dry quickly after rain.
Keep weeds and grass under the vine short.
Fungicides work best from early shoot growth until a few weeks after flowering. Ask an agriculture officer which products are approved.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).cause: A group of wood-rotting fungi, including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium species
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: A trunk disease. The fungi enter through pruning wounds and grow inside the wood for years. The leaf symptoms come from damage inside the vine.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).symptoms: Yellow or reddish stripes between the leaf veins that dry out and turn brown, giving a 'tiger stripe' look. Grapes may develop small dark spots. A vine can also wilt and die suddenly in hot weather.
guidance: There is no cure once the wood is infected.
Prune in dry weather and cover large pruning cuts with a wound sealant.
Cut out and remove dead or infected wood, and do not leave it near the vines.
Mark vines with symptoms and prune them last, so tools do not carry the fungus to healthy vines.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: A fungal leaf disease that is most common in warm, humid regions. It usually appears on older leaves later in the season.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.symptoms: Irregular dark brown spots on the leaves, sometimes with a yellow edge. The spots join into large dead patches, and badly affected leaves fall early.
guidance: Collect and remove fallen leaves.
Prune for airflow so leaves dry quickly.
Avoid overhead watering.
Ask an agriculture officer about approved protective fungicides if the disease spreads.

Grape___healthy.description: No signs of disease were found on this grape leaf.
Grape___healthy.symptoms: The leaf is evenly green with no spots, stripes or dead patches.
guidance: Prune every year to keep the vine open to air and light.
Remove fallen leaves and old fruit from under the vine.
Check leaves often during wet weather.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).cause: Bacterium (Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus), spread by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri)
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: A serious bacterial disease of citrus. A small insect, the Asian citrus psyllid, carries the bacteria from tree to tree. Infected trees decline over a few years.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).symptoms: Blotchy yellow patches on leaves that are different on each side of the main vein. Leaves may be small and stand upright. Fruit is small, lopsided, bitter and stays green at the bottom end.
guidance: There is no cure. Infected trees usually need to be removed so they do not infect others.
Control the psyllid insect on nearby citrus trees.
Buy new plants only from certified disease-free nurseries.
Report suspected cases to the Department of Agriculture.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease of leaves, twigs and fruit. It spreads by rain and wind, and is worse in warm, wet and windy weather.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple or brown. The centres often fall out, leaving 'shot holes'. Leaves turn yellow and drop. Fruit may get small pits or cracks.
guidance: Plant resistant peach varieties where possible.
Avoid too much nitrogen fertiliser.
Keep trees healthy with good pruning and watering, since stressed trees suffer more.
Ask an agriculture officer about copper sprays and the right timing for your area.

Peach___healthy.description: No signs of disease were found on this peach leaf.
Peach___healthy.symptoms: The leaf is evenly green with no spots, holes or yellowing.
guidance: Prune every year to open the centre of the tree.
Water at the base, not over the leaves.
Check leaves after periods of rain and wind.

Raspberry___healthy.description: No signs of disease were found on this raspberry leaf.
Raspberry___healthy.symptoms: The leaf is evenly green with no spots, yellowing or curling.
guidance: Remove old canes after they finish fruiting.
Keep rows narrow so air can move between canes.
Water at the base of the plants.

Soybean___healthy.description: No signs of disease were found on this soybean leaf.
Soybean___healthy.symptoms: The leaf is evenly green with no spots, lesions or yellowing.
guidance: Keep checking the field regularly, especially in humid weather.
Rotate soybean with other crops to reduce disease build-up in the soil.
Use clean, good-quality seed.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: A common fungal disease of squash, pumpkin and cucumber. Unlike most leaf diseases, it does not need wet leaves to spread. Humid air is enough.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White, powdery spots on both sides of the leaves that spread until the whole leaf is covered. Leaves turn yellow, then brown and dry. Fruit may be small or poor in flavour.
guidance: Plant resistant varieties where available.
Space plants so air can move between them.
Remove badly infected leaves.
Ask an agriculture officer about sulphur, potassium bicarbonate or other approved products.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: A fungal leaf disease that spreads by water splash. It survives on old infected leaves.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.symptoms: Many small, irregular, dark purple spots on the upper leaf surface. Unlike common leaf spot, the spots have no pale centre. The spots join until the leaf looks burnt or scorched and dries out.
guidance: Remove and destroy old infected leaves, especially after harvest.
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering.
Do not let plants become overcrowded.
Choose resistant varieties for new plantings.

Strawberry___healthy.description: No signs of disease were found on this strawberry leaf.
Strawberry___healthy.symptoms: The leaf is evenly green with no purple spots or dry patches.
guidance: Water at the base of the plants, ideally in the morning.
Remove old and dead leaves regularly.
Keep space between plants for airflow.

Blueberry___healthy.description: No signs of disease were found on this blueberry leaf.
Blueberry___healthy.symptoms: The leaf is evenly green with no spots, red patches or yellowing between the veins.
guidance: Blueberries need acidic soil. Yellow leaves with green veins can mean the soil pH is too high.
Mulch around the plants to keep the roots moist.
Prune old, weak stems every year.
